We are a student team coming from Turkey as a bunch of tech enthusiasts who were bent on making a difference to the world through rockets, drones and competitions with the goal of leading others with the philosophy of an aviator in hopes to never make mistakes when it matters the most.

summary: Our project EarthTREND is a completely free web tool that lets researchers and developers or the public act as an Earth-system trend detective! On the interface the user can choose one of five NASA POWER variables of their preference (examples being: air temperature, daily maximum temperature, precipitation, root-zone soil wetness or surface sunlight, from the MERRA-2 model and the CERES satellite instruments), and it lets the user see where and how much it has changed as early as the 1990s to as far as the 2050s. Selecting a country on the interactive 3D globe medal will make the country zoom towards you and show you the graph of its yearly series with a trend line and rate per decade, and if the user wants they could also read it in plain words whether it be if the trend is statistically significant (Mann-Kendall test, corrected for runs of similar years) or if its not significant. Statistical forecasts estimate each grid cell up to the year 2050. Our project is aimed to address the challenges need to show trends and not just that we also aim to show how the crops are going to get effected from these trends.
details: Our project EarthTREND is a static website built using the coding languages HTML, CSS, JavaScript and the three.js 3D library, it is currently being hosted on the GitHub Pages with all the calculations being run in the visitor’s browser, and to protect privacy nothing is stored about visitors information, and it works offline except for the close-up satellite imagery which the browser needs to load directly from NASA GIBS. The simulation system first requires the user to pick a variable from NASA POWER (MERRA-2 reanalysis and CERES sunlight) options with each one containing a one-line plain definition and making the globe color every single cell by its change since the first five years of the chosen range or by its value which just depends on what the user has chosen through the interface. Temperature and rain data are shown on 5° cells built using the monthly data but daily maximum temperature, soil wetness and sunlight also have sharper 0.5° grids that load when chosen. Selecting a country on the 3D globe model draws its yearly series change alongside a trend line and rate per decade with a sentence that says whether the rise or fall could be considered scientifically significant. The system uses the Mann-Kendall test with the Hamed-Rao correction for runs of similar years while leaving out partly measured years (1990 temperature and 2026) and forecast years. The timeline is able to run up to 2050 where each cell’s forecast is its seasonal cycle combined with the level of the last 20 years plus a trend averaged by its neighbouring cells it has an 80 % range for natural year-to-year swings. When the 2017-2025 datasets sets were hidden and was being forecast from 1991-2016 instead, the error margin was only 0.593 °C for temperature and 197.8 mm per year for rain, against 0.616 °C and 201.4 mm for a straight line, and the real values were inside the range 74 % of the time for temperature dataset and 79 % for the rain dataset. The crop detector is able to cover up to 136 countries and currently features seven crops (wheat, maize, rice, soybeans, barley, sorghum, millet) and it assigns each crop a chance that the 2025 harvest falls at least 10 % below its own trend. It is a random-forest machine-learning model trained offline in Python with scikit-learn (LightGBM and other models were compared but could not beat the current model therefore they were not used), using past FAOSTAT harvests, NASA POWER weather and soil in the three months before the season, NOAA vegetation health, El Niño and five other ocean and air cycles from NOAA, and irrigation share from the World Bank. Trained on 1986-2010 and tested on 2011-2024, it ranks risky crops better than a simple formula such as AUC 0.73 against 0.70 but picks the bad year inside a country only slightly better than chance, and its chances run about 4 points high because shortfalls became rarer after 2010. The intended impact of this project is that anyone can investigate what is changing, where, how much and whether it is significant, and see which harvests in which countries are most at risk, and we aim to achieve creativity and originality through our approach to this problem whether it be the crop estimation or how we present our trend estimation. Our team has also considered failure factors such as extreme changes and spikes in data but our approach has been to detect the overall trend instead of trying to guess what it would be in a specific date.
